text:
Species-specific variation in 
predicted distribution and habitat 
suitability of phlebotomine sand 
flies in Italy under different climate 
change scenarios
Camila González1, Johan Manuel Calderón1, Ana María López1, Ilaria Bernardini2, 
Luigi Gradoni2, Marco Pombi3, Gioia Bongiorno2 & Simona Gabrielli3
The incidence of human and canine leishmaniasis in Europe is increasing and is a key indicator in the 
Lancet Countdown report on health and climate change 2024. While the potential distribution of 
the disease on a continental scale has been assessed under climate change scenarios, local analyses 
of vector species distribution are crucial for effective prevention strategies. Italy is endemic for 
Leishmania infantum, and expansions in the latitudinal and altitudinal distribution of canine cases and 
vector species have been recorded. This study evaluated the potential distribution of six phlebotomine 
sand fly species, known or suspected vectors of L. infantum, under climate change scenarios using 
ecological niche modeling and the maximum entropy (MaxEnt v. 3.4.1) modeling algorithm. We 
analyzed 410 records from 1979 to 2013 and projected future distributions for 2041–2060 and 
2061–2080 using five CMIP5 models and two representative concentration pathways. Historical data 
from 1968 to 1972 were also examined to confirm suitable areas. The predictions indicate suitable 
habitats for sand flies throughout Italy, and variations among the different scenarios evaluated. All 
species show potential for expansion, such as the main vector, P. perniciosus, which shows an increase 
in the percentage of suitable habitat over time. On the other hand, predictions for P. perfiliewi don’t 
show a clear pattern, with an initial decrease and subsequent increase in suitable areas. Shifts in the 
distribution of insect vectors may affect the dynamics of Leishmania transmission, highlighting the 
need for improved surveillance strategies.
Leishmaniases are a group of climate-sensitive vector-borne infectious diseases that in Europe are predominantly 
caused by Leishmania infantum (Kinetoplastida, Trypanosomatidae), which causes visceral (VL) and cutaneous 
(CL) syndromes in humans and animals1 of which dogs are the main reservoir in the Mediterranean area.
Leishmaniases are transmitted by phlebotomine sand flies belonging to the genera Phlebotomus (Old World) 
and Lutzomyia(New World)2. Among these, L. infantum, the main etiological agent of canine and human 
leishmaniasis, is endemic throughout the Mediterranean basin3, where it is responsible for both visceral (VL) 
and cutaneous (CL) manifestations in humans and animals1.
In Italy, its transmission is predominantly mediated by sand flies of the Larroussius subgenus, particularly 
Phlebotomus perniciosus (Newstead, 1911) and Phlebotomus perfiliewi (Parrot, 1930), which are recognized as the 
primary proven vectors4,5. Nevertheless, the Italian phlebotomine fauna includes several other species, such as 
Phlebotomus ariasi (Tonnoir, 1921), Phlebotomus mascittii (Grassi, 1908), Phlebotomus neglectus (Tonnoir, 1921), 
Phlebotomus papatasi (Scopoli, 1786), Phlebotomus sergenti (Parrot, 1917), and Sergentomyia minuta(Rondani, 
1843)5,6. Of these, P. perniciosus, P. perfiliewi, P. ariasi, and P. neglectus are proven or suspected vectors of L. 
infantum, and P. perniciosus  is the main vector of the parasite4,5,7–9. Notably, Sergentomyia minuta, which

primarily feeds on ectothermic hosts such as lizards10 and transmits Leishmania (Sauroleishmania) tarentolae, 
has recently received particular attention following reports of L. infantum DNA in sand flies of this genus11–14.
Leishmaniases have been included as one of three new indicators in the 2024 Europe report of the Lancet 
Countdown on health and climate change15. In Europe, the number of reported cases has increased both in 
humans and dogs, and risk areas have been defined to assess the potential of disease spreading under global 
climate and land cover changes16–18. However, significant variations in incidence rates have been observed 
over different periods and increases in incidence in certain European countries contrast with fluctuations or 
declines in others1. Such changes in incidence are linked to human demographic shifts, societal changes, and 
environmental factors. Decreases in visceral leishmaniasis (VL) incidence, for example, have been associated 
with improvements in living standards wherein better nutrition can mitigate infant fatalities caused by VL19.
In humans, the WHO estimates between 1100 and 1900 cases per 100,000 individuals, while in dogs, which 
are highly susceptible and important reservoirs, a seroprevalence of 10% has been consistently found in Western 
Europe20. In Italy the seroprevalence of L. infantum is higher, reaching up to 20%, making it the country with the 
highest incidence of canine leishmaniasis (CanL) in Europe1. Stable endemic foci of CanL have been reported 
from central and southern regions, including the islands of Sicily and Sardinia21. However, in recent years L. 
infantum and its vectors have spread from traditional endemic areas of southern and insular regions to central 
and northern parts of the country16,22,23.
Climate change is recognized for inducing shifts in species distributions along both altitudinal and latitudinal 
gradients (IPPC6). These environmental changes significantly impact vector habitats and alter the dynamics 
of disease transmission1. Many studies have suggested the potential of a northward spread of sandflies with 
increasing temperatures; however, little is known regarding its potential altitudinal variation in temperate 
regions. Previous models of the potential spatial distribution of leishmaniasis in North America in response 
to climate change showed a potential increase in distribution areas in a latitudinal gradient, possibly favoring 
the spread of the disease to more temperate regions24. In tropical regions, there is a general trend of increased 
altitudinal distribution and reduced area of distribution through time, predicting some regions of potential local 
extinctions due to habitat unsuitability25.
Furthermore, the establishment of new transmission cycles in urban and peri-urban areas is of significant 
concern. Urbanization and land use changes have contributed to the adaptation and spread of Leishmania vectors. 
Despite its widespread occurrence across several European countries, including Italy, Spain, and France, the 
disease is often neglected and underreported, uncovering gaps in surveillance systems1. These regions exhibit 
notable endemicity for both CL and VL1. For instance, the transmission of L. infantum is closely related to 
urbanization and changes in land cover, which facilitate the establishment of vectors and the subsequent trigger 
of transmission cycles. The introduction of L. infantum into previously non-endemic areas may result from 
increased dog movement, such as the importation of infected dogs, and environmental changes that create 
suitable microhabitats for sand flies22.
Although the potential distribution of leishmaniasis in Europe has been assessed under climate change 
scenarios, smaller-scale analyses focusing on vector distribution are crucial to identify high-risk areas for 
new transmission zones and to inform the development of effective preventive actions and control strategies. 
Therefore, our primary objective was to assess the dispersal potential of L. infantum vectors in Italy under 
contrasting climate change scenarios using ecological niche modeling. Specifically, we evaluated five future 
CMIP5 models obtained from CHELSA26, and for each model two periods were projected (2041–2060 and 
2061–2080), with two Representative Concentration Pathways (RCPs), 4.5 and 8.5. Additionally, we contribute

information about the historical distribution of sand fly species, and compare these records with the future 
distribution, based on the climatic scenarios.
Results
Species distribution modeling
From 1979 to 2013, we obtained 807 records belonging to P. perniciosus (n = 323), P. perfiliewi (n = 129), P. 
neglectus (n = 85), P. papatasi (n = 54), P. mascittii (n = 47), P. ariasi (n = 8), P. sergenti (n = 6) and S. minuta (n = 155) 
(Fig. 1). To build the models we excluded P. ariasi and P. sergenti due to their low number of occurrences. After 
depuration and filtering, we obtained a final dataset including six species (P. perniciosus, P. perfiliewi, P. neglectus, 
P. papatasi, P. mascittii, and S. minuta) with 410 records. Table 1 summarizes the performance statistics for the 
four SDMs for each species. We constructed binary maps using the 10% training percentile threshold. Final 
continuous and uncertainty maps can be found in Supplementary Fig. S1 to S6. We selected the best model for 
each species based on a high performance of (i) pAUC ratios and (ii) omission rates. The pAUC ratio should be 
greater than one, meaning that the model has a higher discriminative ability than a null model, which assigns 
presences randomly in the background area. Omission rates should be close to zero for OR0 and close to 0.10 
or lower for OR10, indicating the proportion of records from the test dataset that were left out of the predicted 
presence area.
Maps were created with ArcGIS Pro 3.4.0 (https://www.arcgis.com/index.html) licensed to the Universidad 
de Los Andes.
According to the obtained SDM, suitable habitats for the presence of sand flies are distributed in all regions 
(Fig. 1, S1-S6). A habitat was considered suitable for a species based on the summary binary maps constructed 
with the OR10 binary outputs (see Methods: Spatial distribution models). The species with the widest suitable 
area was P. perniciosus (61.56% of the country), whereas the one with the most restricted predicted area was P. 
mascittii (27.29%), for which suitability areas are predominant in the northern and the central regions of Italy 
and mostly absent from the insular regions (see Supplementary Fig. S1). However, it must be noted that Sardinia 
has historical records of presence that were not included in the models. Spatial predictions for P. neglectus include 
mainly the North and Insular regions, with coastal areas suitable along the entire Peninsula (see Supplementary

Alps and the Apennine mountains is predicted as suitable (see Supplementary Fig. S3), while P. perfiliewii is 
predicted to occur in the Central, South, and Insular regions (see Supplementary Fig. S4), and P. perniciosus in 
all the country except the highlands (see Supplementary Fig. S5). Sergentomyia minuta is predicted to occur in 
all regions but Emilia-Romagna and Basilicata (see Supplementary Fig. S6).
Even though habitat suitability was found in Sardinia for P. neglectus and P. papatasi, the occurrence of those 
species has not yet been reported in this island. Suitable areas for most of the phlebotomine species were mainly 
located in Piedmont, central Lombardy, coastal Veneto, Tuscany, Latium, Marche, Abruzzo, coastal Campania, 
southern Calabria, and eastern Sicily (Fig. 2). On the contrary, unsuitable areas for phlebotomine species were 
especially located in the highland regions (Fig. 2).

Future scenarios
Regarding predictions in the future, in general, there was variation among the predictions of the five CMIP5 
models for the areas of predicted presence per species. The area of predicted presence corresponded to the 
proportion of pixels suitable for a species inside the entire calibration area (Italian territory). A pixel was 
considered suitable if its predicted probability in the future scenarios was higher than the OR10 threshold for 
the present. Consistent patterns through the two future intervals (2041–2060 and 2061–2080) were observed 
only in certain species and scenarios. The patterns described for each species were based on the consensus of at 
least three CMIP5 models.
Under the stabilization scenario (RCP 4.5), all species exhibit areas of potential expansion, but also some 
areas for loss (see Supplementary Fig. S7 and Table S2 for the percentage of gained or lost area for each 
species). By species, P. mascittii would remain present in the north and the western central coast with a possible 
expansion to the northern areas (see Supplementary Fig. S7A, B); P. neglectus would remain present in the 
northern and southern regions, Sicily and Sardinia, with some areas of expansion (see Supplementary Fig. S7C, 
D); P. papatasi would persist in most of the country showing potential expansion towards the central highlands 
(see Supplementary Fig. S7E, F); P. perfiliewi would persist in the central and insular regions with a potential 
expansion towards southern Apulia (see Supplementary Fig. S7G, H); P. perniciosus would remain in most of the 
territory with expansion mostly in the central region (see Supplementary Fig. S7I, J); S. minuta would persist in 
the north, the western coast and the islands but without a clear expansion trend (see Supplementary Fig. S7K, L).
Under the high CO2 emissions scenario (RCP 8.5), a potential increase in the distribution range was also 
predicted for all species, being P. papatasi the one with the greatest expansion potential (see Supplementary 
Fig. S8). For P. perfiliewi and P. neglectus, the predicted area is very variable between CMIP5 models, and no 
consensus was found, showing areas of gain and loss for the two periods (see Supplementary Fig. S8). By species, 
P. mascittii will have the same trend as in the RCP 4.5; P. neglectus shows a greater potential expansion towards

Discussion
Assessing the spatial distribution of species involved in transmitting vector-borne diseases under climate change 
is crucial for designing effective prevention strategies and preparing for outbreaks. However, adequate species 
distribution modeling (SDM) faces challenges due to limitations in data availability and variations in algorithm 
performance. The MaxEnt algorithm is widely favored for its capability to handle presence-only data along 
with its high accuracy, flexibility, and robustness. MaxEnt has been shown to outperform other models, like 
GARP, providing niche models with greater accuracy27,28and greater performance to predict habitat changes 
due to climate change29. Moreover, it is robust to collinearity during model training, meaning it can handle 
redundant variables without significant loss of performance30. Considering limitations, MaxEnt has shown lower 
performance when compared to algorithms that use both presence and absence data31. However, this limitation 
would be based more on the quality of information provided to the algorithm by the use of absences compared 
to the use of background points. In addition, the output style of MaxEnt models may differ from other modeling 
frameworks, making direct comparisons difficult. This can lead to confusion in interpretation32. Ensuring clarity 
and consistency in model output is critical for effective application.
Entomological surveillance, particularly for medically important species, remains uneven across countries33, 
with most data limited to small-scale studies aimed at understanding local dynamics within specific time 
periods. Maps generated often provide a broad overview of species distribution based on political boundaries

(e.g., ECDC, ​h​t​t​p​s​:​/​/​w​w​w​.​e​c​d​c​.​e​u​r​o​p​a​.​e​u​/​e​n​/​d​i​s​e​a​s​e​-​v​e​c​t​o​r​s​/​s​u​r​v​e​i​l​l​a​n​c​e​-​a​n​d​-​d​i​s​e​a​s​e​-​d​a​t​a​/​p​h​l​e​b​o​t​o​m​i​n​e​-​m​a​p​
s). Raster binary maps of potential distribution, such as those produced in this work, complement traditional 
surveillance by integrating biological and ecological factors, enhancing the assessment of at-risk areas. This study 
aimed to evaluate the dispersal potential of sand fly species in Italy, focusing on the main vectors of L. infantum, 
using ecological niche modeling. This approach builds upon previous efforts that mapped P. perniciosus potential 
distribution in northeastern Italy using retrospective entomological survey data from 2001 to 201234.
Our findings align with ECDC maps depicting the current distribution of Phlebotomus  species across 
Europe1. Suitable habitats for L. infantum vectors were identified in all Italian regions except highlands. 
Specifically, P. perniciosus exhibited the widest distribution, followed by P. perfiliewii and P. papatasi. However, 
future projections diverged from previous studies indicating a northward expansion of Leishmania vectors under 
climate change scenarios35. Whereas all species showed potential expansion, outcomes varied significantly across 
the five CMIP5 models considered. This underscores the critical importance of employing robust methodologies 
that compare multiple scenarios and project both optimistic and pessimistic outcomes. Such an approach not 
only enhances the reliability of predictions but also provides valuable insights into the range of possible futures 
under different climate change scenarios, aiding in more informed decision-making for disease prevention and 
control strategies.

Focusing on the primary Leishmania vectors, P. perniciosus was predicted to expand into central highlands, 
whereas P. perfiliewi showed potential expansion towards southern regions under the stabilization scenario 
(RCP 4.5), with mixed outcomes under the high emission scenario (RCP 8.5). Predictions for P. neglectus were 
highly variable among models, lacking consensus. This suggests surveillance will play a key role to monitor this 
species and its potential distribution under climate change scenarios.
The predicted habitat suitability for P. papatasi exceeded observed distributions based on our records. This 
species, known for its indoor presence in domestic and peridomestic settings, may expand across the entire 
country except for northern highlands. While it serves as the main vector for L. major in the Mediterranean, the 
parasite itself is not endemic in Europe36, suggesting potential for colonization under climate change scenarios.
Considering the natural shifts in species distributions, human-mediated introductions warrant careful 
assessment. In the case of leishmaniasis, the movement of infected reservoir hosts, primarily dogs, poses a risk for 
establishing new transmission foci in non-endemic areas, potentially involving competent sand fly species (e.g., 
L. donovani and L. tropica)20,37,38. Vigilance and entomological surveillance are essential to detect Leishmania 
vectors in non-endemic regions and to monitor disease cases to prevent new foci from emerging.
Recent studies have highlighted S. minuta’s potential role as a vector for human Leishmania spp., despite its 
preference for reptilian hosts12–14. Our study confirms its wide distribution and predicts expansions in various 
regions of Italy, reinforcing the need for surveillance due to its suspected role in L. infantum transmission39.

Not all the species were present in both datasets: P. ariasi was absent in the historical dataset, P. mascittii, 
was present in Sardinia from 1969 to 1972, but absent from 1979 to 2013 and P. sergenti was found in Sicily only 
from 1979 to 2013. This underscores the importance of historical records to adequately assess whether areas of 
potential distribution actually have expansion potential or information gaps.
Climate change drives significant shifts in medically important species distributions, as emphasized by the 
IPCC’s assessment of disease and vector range expansions into higher latitudes and elevations40,41. Monitoring 
regions conducive to vector presence is critical for preventing disease outbreaks in densely populated areas 
with susceptible populations. Our findings underscore the influence of environmental and climate factors on 
leishmaniasis vector distribution and demonstrate the usefulness of ecological niche modeling to predict disease 
spread. While predictions vary among CMIP5 models, overall trends suggest that rising temperatures will likely 
favor species expansions both spatially and altitudinally. Moving forward, integrating ecological niche modeling 
with experimental studies could enhance our understanding of vector biology and disease dynamics.
Conclusions
Sand fly species of medical importance are already widely distributed in Italy, and this scenario will inevitably 
change, based on future projections. In a context of preparedness, based on the predicted future distributions, 
studies on species composition and local abundances should be addressed in areas where one or more sand fly 
vectors are expected, so that the risk of establishment of new transmission foci can be properly evaluated.
This study clearly indicates that under climate change scenarios, significant differences between regions are 
expected for all sand fly vectors of Italian fauna. Despite species-specific changes in countrywide distribution, 
a general trend of expansion is expected. In addition to this, as other studies have reported, an expansion of 
potential areas of distribution for sand fly species along an altitudinal gradient is expected to occur. Therefore, 
studies are needed at a national scale to better understand the impact of altitudinal changes in Leishmania 
spp. transmission in areas where it was not present in the past. This spatial and altitudinal trend will certainly 
affect the epidemiology of L. infantum in both humans and animals, highlighting the need for a continuous 
improvement of coordinated effort to associate vector surveillance with reporting of clinical cases at regional 
and countrywide scale.
Methods
Species distribution modeling
In order to evaluate the current and future potential distribution, the time frame of the records was defined from 
1979 to 2013 to match the available bioclimatic coverages. We used information obtained through a systematic 
review conducted by the Istituto Superiore di Sanità42, which included information from 1975 to 2009 and 
was obtained through published articles retrieved from various search engines (PubMED-MEDLINE, LIBIS, 
BIBSYS, SBN-OPAC, ScienceDirect, Bibliothèque Nationale de France, British Library, GBV, Library of Congress, 
OvidSP, CABI, and Google Scholar), as well as from various institutional portals of research and territorial 
control agencies (local health authorities, experimental zooprophylactic institutes, regional environmental 
protection agencies, universities). The search included different combinations of species and genus names, both 
common and Latin, as well as geographical delimitation criteria (Italy only) and temporal criteria (only articles 
published or data collected between January 1, 1985, and December 31, 2009). In addition, data were collected 
from non-indexed publications such as conference proceedings, graduate or doctoral theses, service reports, 
and others. The collected bibliographic citations were entered into an online archive using the RefWorks© 
platform for individual analysis. The data were extracted only if the relevant geographical information (at least 
the municipality) and the year of collection were available. Incomplete or inaccurate reports were not included. 
Records from 2009 to 2013 were obtained from published articles retrieved from PubMed using the following 
search terms: “sand fly species” AND “presence” AND “Italy”. The database was curated to remove locations with 
missing coordinates or incorrect georeferencing, and we included eight species in the analyses (Phlebotomus 
ariasi, P. mascittii, P. neglectus, P. papatasi, P. perfiliewi, P. perniciosus, P. sergenti, and S. minuta). The data 
analyzed in this study are included as Supplementary Information files.
The 19 bioclimatic variables derived from CHELSA comprising climate variability from 1979 to 2013 were

used (https://chelsa-climate.org/bioclim/)26. These coverages have a spatial resolution of 0.00833 decimal 
degrees (approximately 1 km). To reduce dimensionality and avoid collinearity, a principal component analysis

(PCA) was performed for the environmental variables using the NicheA software v.3.043 and the first five PCs 
were chosen for distribution modeling (96.66% of total variation).
To reduce the effect of sampling bias in the dataset, data filtering in the geographic and the environmental 
space were compared. In the geographic space, spatial thinning was performed with the spThin R package44 
using two minimum nearest neighbor distances of 1 and 5 km. In the environmental space, data filtering was 
carried out by sampling 80% of occurrences within the minimum volume ellipsoid (MVE) including all the 
records. To do this, two methods available in the NicheA software were used: a threshold method (software 
selects occurrences randomly according to the threshold β = 0.7) and a probability method (software converts 
the probabilities according to a logistic function of threshold β = 0.7 and slope α = −0.05, and samples based on 
the converted probability. Areas with high probability contain more occurrences).
Spatial distribution models (SDM) were run for each species and the calibration area used was the entire 
territory of Italy. The selected modeling algorithm was the maximum entropy (MaxEnt v.3.4.1)45The MaxEnt 
algorithm is widely favored for its capability to handle presence-only data along with its high accuracy, flexibility, 
and robustness. MaxEnt has been shown to outperform other models, like GARP, providing niche models with 
greater accuracy27,28 and greater performance to predict habitat changes due to climate change29. Moreover, it is 
robust to collinearity during model training, meaning it can handle redundant variables without significant loss 
of performance30.
The used settings were: 10,000 background points, 500 iterations, and log-log output. Five regularization 
coefficients (0.02, 0.1, 0.46, 1, 2.2 and 4.6) and three feature classes (linear, quadratic and product) were tested 
for each species using the ENMeval  R package46; the combination producing the lowest corrected Akaike 
information criterion (AICc) was selected (see Supplementary Table S1). For each species, ENMs were run 10 
times with different presence samples to test robustness47, and model evaluation was performed each time. In 
each repetition, 80% of the occurrences were randomly chosen for training the model and the remaining 20% 
of the occurrences were used for testing. Two evaluation methods were carried out: partial area under the ROC 
curve (pAUC)48and omission rates49. The pAUC with errors of 0.10 and 0.50 and their ratio to the AUC null 
model were calculated for each repetition (performed with NicheA). Ten-percentile (OR10) and zero-percentile 
(OR0) omission rates, which were the proportion of testing occurrences omitted with each training threshold, 
were calculated along with their predicted presence area (obtained from MaxEnt).
For each species, a continuous map was built using the mean of the 10 obtained continuous outputs (from 
the 10 repetitions), and an uncertainty map using the standard deviation of those outputs. Lastly, a binary 
map was constructed using the raster R package summing the OR10 binary outputs obtained from the ten 
repetitions; pixels with predicted presence in five or more of the binary outputs were considered “suitable” while 
the remaining were considered “unsuitable”.
Future scenarios
Five future CMIP5 models obtained from CHELSA26were chosen based on their lowest amount of 
interdependence50: CESM1-BGC, CESM1-CAM5, CMCC-CM, MIROC5, and MPI-ESM-MR. For each model, 
SDMs were projected for two periods (2041–2060 and 2061–2080), with two Representative Concentration 
Pathways (RCPs), 4.5 and 8.5. The RCP 4.5 is a stabilization scenario, which means the radiative forcing level 
stabilizes at 4.5 W/m2 before the year 2100 due to the implementation of a range of technologies and strategies

aiming to reduce greenhouse gas emissions. In the RCP 8.5, the radiative forcing level reaches 8.5  W/m2 
characterized by increasing greenhouse gas emissions over time, leading to high greenhouse gas concentration 
levels.
Model transfer to future scenarios was carried out by doing, first, a model with the entire set of occurrences 
(all the available information) and the same regularization coefficients and feature classes as the present SDMs. 
Those present models were projected to future CMIP5 scenarios. The previously performed PCA with the 
environmental variables for the present was transferred to the future scenarios using NicheA. Lastly, the first five 
PCs were used for model projections, which were done with MaxEnt.
To assess the spatial variation predicted by the two RCP and the five CMIP5 models, the outputs were 
visualized, where binary outputs were summed to obtain the present-day areas of presence and absence, and 
predicted areas of expansion and reduction51. To evaluate elevational changes, the percentage of suitable habitat 
per elevation class (each 100 m from 0 to 4300 masl) was calculated for each species using Eq. (1).
	
Percentage of suitable habitat = Suitable pixels in an elevation class
Total pixels in the elevation class
X 100 
(1)
This calculation was carried out for the present, and for the future periods, 2041–2060 and 2061–2080.
Sand fly historical distribution
To revise if areas with no records for modeling but predicted as of potential distribution are true absences, we 
used unpublished data from field work notebooks containing collection records from 1968 to 1972 from the 
Parasitology Laboratory at the Department of Public Health and Infectious Diseases of Sapienza University 
(Rome, Italy). Fieldwork information was digitized in a database and for each record the following fields were 
included: species, collection date, province, municipality, locality, and capture site. Records were georeferenced 
using Google Maps and distribution maps were built using ArcMap (version 10.2 for windows licensed to 
Universidad de Los Andes, Colombia).
Data availability
Data is provided within the manuscript or supplementary information files.
